facet_selection_reasoning: This combination targets the fundamental conceptual understanding of what a confidence interval represents and how its confidence level should be interpreted. By combining A4 and A5 with B15 and B16, the item can distinguish between students who understand CIs as a frequentist procedure for capturing population parameters and those who incorrectly view them as probability statements about specific intervals or as descriptors of sample data.

item.stem: A researcher conducted a study on the sleep habits of college students. Based on a random sample of 100 students, she calculated a 95% confidence interval for the population mean sleep time to be (6.4, 7.2) hours. Determine whether each of the following statements is a correct or incorrect interpretation of this confidence interval.

options.text: We are 95% confident that the population mean sleep time for all college students is between 6.4 and 7.2 hours.
options.rationale: This is a correct interpretation of the confidence interval, focusing on the population parameter and using the standard definition of confidence.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the population mean sleep time is between 6.4 and 7.2 hours.
options.rationale: This is incorrect because it interprets confidence as a probability for a fixed interval. In frequentist statistics, the population mean is a fixed value and the interval is either right or wrong; there is no probability for a single calculated interval.

options.text: If we repeated this study many times and calculated a 95% confidence interval for each sample, approximately 95% of those intervals would capture the true population mean.
options.rationale: This correctly describes the frequentist definition of confidence as the long-run success rate of the interval-building process across many replications.

options.text: Approximately 95% of all college students in the population sleep between 6.4 and 7.2 hours.
options.rationale: This is incorrect because it confuses the confidence interval for the mean with a range that captures individual scores or data points within the population.

options.text: We are 95% confident that the mean sleep time of the 100 students in the sample is between 6.4 and 7.2 hours.
options.rationale: This is incorrect because a confidence interval is used to estimate unknown population parameters, not the sample statistic, which is already known and always located at the center of the interval.

item.explanation: This item assesses students' ability to interpret confidence intervals correctly by distinguishing the population parameter from sample statistics and individual data. Correct interpretations (opt_1 and opt_3) emphasize the population mean and the long-run frequency of the estimation process (A4, A5). Incorrect interpretations address the common probability fallacy (B15 in opt_2) and the confusion between estimating population means versus sample statistics or individual scores (B16 in opt_4 and opt_5).

This explicitly states the probability misconception for a single confidence interval, which perfectly aligns with B15.
This is the classic frequentist definition of confidence level involving replications (A4), and it correctly identifies that the interval seeks to capture the population mean (A5).
The option wrongly interprets the confidence interval as capturing individual scores (data points/true scores) instead of the population parameter, which aligns closely with B16.
This option illustrates the misconception that a confidence interval is used to estimate a sample statistic (the sample mean), which is an exact match for B16.
